items.title: Labarbera interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2021
items.q: Maybe Miles’ first solo he stayed pretty strict into the D minor

ctx.x: If you’re teaching a student and they are, let’s supposed they’re playing on “So What.” And they’re obviously missing the half-step change. My question is about wrong notes. What term do you use with them with — I mean wrong notes now seems to be a thing like well don’t call them wrong notes. So how do you approach them with — you’re playing wrong notes. That’s the best I can say.

Yeah what I do is I actually make students play wrong notes. I’ll do a tune like “So What” and I’ll just say okay, let’s figure out the notes that are going to sound bad on D minor seventh, okay? Let’s figure the notes that are going to be something, and let’s work on hitting that note. E flat. Right? Okay, and F sharp on the D minor seven chord. Let’s practice hitting those notes, first of all to get rid of the fear of hitting a wrong note. Because that’s one thing that keeps people from going, keeps them from…

went out, in and out of the chord, up or low, the neighbor tones, there’s so many devices, with Trane it was superimposed “Giant Steps” changes over it before he would come back in. But there was so much theory there, but it all came from the fact that if you want to play the Dorian mode in a church setting the way those church modes, fine. You stay in the mode in a traditional way of speaking. But nobody ever plays that way when you’re playing.
